content.question: In which year was the Indian National Congress established?
content.note: The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded in December 1885. Its first session was held at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay (Mumbai).

content.question: What was significant about the Lahore Session (1929)?
content.answer: Demand for complete independence (Purna Swaraj) was passed
content.note: Presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, the 1929 Lahore Session was historic because the Congress passed the resolution for Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence) and decided to celebrate Jan 26 as Independence Day.

content.question: Who founded the Brahmo Samaj?
content.note: Raja Ram Mohan Roy, the 'Father of Indian Renaissance', founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828 to promote monotheism and social reforms like the abolition of Sati.

content.question: Why did Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement?
content.answer: Due to the Chauri Chaura incident
content.note: In 1922, a violent mob set fire to a police station in Chauri Chaura (UP), killing 22 policemen. Committed to non-violence, Mahatma Gandhi immediately called off the Non-Cooperation Movement.

content.question: The Dandi March is associated with which movement?
content.note: The Dandi March (Salt Satyagraha) of 1930, where Gandhi marched to the coast to make salt, marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement against British salt laws.

content.question: Who formulated the Doctrine of Lapse?
content.note: Lord Dalhousie used the Doctrine of Lapse to annex princely states (like Satara, Jhansi, and Nagpur) if the ruler died without a natural male heir.

content.question: Where did Gandhi launch his first Satyagraha in India?
content.note: After returning from South Africa, Gandhi's first major movement in India was the Champaran Satyagraha (1917) in Bihar, supporting indigo farmers against the Tinkathia system.

content.question: Who gave the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright"?
content.note: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a prominent extremist leader, famously declared: "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it!" He used festivals like Ganpati and Shivaji Utsav to mobilize the masses.

content.question: Who founded the All India Muslim League?
content.note: The All India Muslim League was formed on December 30, 1906, in Dhaka (now Bangladesh) under the leadership of Nawab Salimullah and Aga Khan III.

content.question: When was the Battle of Plassey fought?
content.note: The Battle of Plassey took place on June 23, 1757. It was a decisive victory for the British East India Company under Robert Clive against the Nawab of Bengal.

content.question: Who led the Bardoli Satyagraha?
content.note: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) in Gujarat against unjust land revenue hikes. The success of this movement earned him the title 'Sardar'.

content.question: Who was called the Father of Local Self-Government?
content.note: Lord Ripon is known as the 'Father of Local Self-Government' in India because he introduced the Resolution of 1882, which laid the foundation for municipal boards and local bodies.

content.question: Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal?
content.note: Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal following the Regulating Act of 1773. He centralized the administration and established the dual system of governance.

content.question: Who founded the Asiatic Society?
content.note: Sir William Jones, a philologist, founded the Asiatic Society in Calcutta in 1784 to encourage and facilitate Oriental research and the study of Indian history and culture.

content.question: In which year was the Lucknow Pact signed?
content.note: The Lucknow Pact was an agreement signed in 1916 between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League to pressure the British for political reforms and communal representation.

content.question: Who led the Revolt of 1857 in Bihar?
content.note: During the Great Revolt of 1857, Veer Kunwar Singh, the 80-year-old Zamindar of Jagdispur, led the rebellion in Bihar and fought valiantly against British forces.

content.question: Who was the first president of the Indian National Congress?
content.note: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee) was a prominent barrister who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress in Bombay in 1885.

content.question: Who abolished Sati in 1829?
content.note: Through the Sati Regulation Act of 1829, Lord William Bentinck (with strong support from Raja Ram Mohan Roy) legally abolished the practice of Sati across British India.

content.question: In which year was the East India Company established?
content.note: The East India Company (EIC) was granted a Royal Charter by Queen Elizabeth I on December 31, 1600, giving them a monopoly on trade with the East Indies.

content.question: What was the first major victory of the East India Company in India?
content.note: The Battle of Plassey (1757) is considered the first major victory for the EIC, as it effectively established British political and military supremacy in Bengal.

content.question: Who betrayed Siraj-ud-Daulah in the Battle of Plassey?
content.note: Mir Jafar, the commander-in-chief of the Nawab's army, entered into a secret pact with the British and withheld his troops during the Battle of Plassey, leading to the defeat of Siraj-ud-Daulah.

content.question: In which year was the First Battle of Panipat fought?
content.note: The First Battle of Panipat was fought on April 21, 1526 CE. It marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.

content.question: In which year was the Lahore Session of INC held?
content.note: The Lahore Session of 1929 is famous for the Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence) declaration. It was presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru on the banks of the Ravi River.

content.question: In which year was the Satyashodhak Samaj founded?
content.note: Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth Seekers' Society) was founded in 1873 by Jyotirao Phule in Maharashtra to fight against caste discrimination and advocate for the rights of Shudras and Dalits.

content.question: Who introduced the Permanent Settlement system in 1793?
content.note: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal and Bihar in 1793. This system fixed land revenue permanently and created a new class of landlords known as Zamindars.

content.question: In which year did Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
content.note: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India on January 9, 1915, after staying in South Africa for 21 years. This day is now celebrated as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (NRI Day).

content.question: Who founded the Arya Samaj?
content.note: Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875. He gave the slogan 'Back to the Vedas' and emphasized monotheism and social reform through education.

content.question: Who founded the Ghadar Party?
content.answer: Lala Hardayal and Sohan Singh Bhakna
content.note: The Ghadar Party was an international political movement founded by expatriate Indians, notably Lala Hardayal and Sohan Singh Bhakna, to overthrow British rule in India using armed force.

content.question: In which year was the Ramakrishna Mission established?
content.note: The Ramakrishna Mission was established in 1897 by Swami Vivekananda to spread the teachings of his guru, Ramakrishna Paramahansa, and to perform social service.

content.question: Who divided Bengal in 1905?
content.note: Lord Curzon carried out the Partition of Bengal in 1905, citing administrative convenience, though the real motive was to weaken the nationalist movement by dividing Hindus and Muslims.

content.question: During which movement did Gandhi give the slogan "Do or Die"?
content.note: During the Quit India Movement (1942), Mahatma Gandhi gave the iconic 'Do or Die' (Karo Ya Maro) speech at Mumbai, demanding an immediate end to British rule.

content.question: Who founded the Prarthana Samaj?
content.answer: Atmaram Pandurang with Keshav Chandra Sen
content.note: The Prarthana Samaj (Prayer Society) was founded in 1867 in Bombay by Atmaram Pandurang. It was influenced by the Brahmo Samaj and worked toward religious and social reforms.

content.question: What was the name of the organization founded by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan?
content.note: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as 'Frontier Gandhi,' founded the Khudai Khidmatgar ('Servants of God'). They were a non-violent Pashtun movement known as the 'Red Shirts'.

content.question: Who founded the Swaraj Party in 1923 along with Motilal Nehru?
content.note: After the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement, Chittaranjan (C.R.) Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party in 1923 to enter the legislative councils and disrupt British governance from within.

content.question: In which year was the partition of Bengal announced?
content.note: The Partition of Bengal was officially announced in 1905. This led to the Swadeshi Movement, marked by the boycott of British goods and the promotion of Indian-made products.

content.question: Who signed the Poona Pact with Mahatma Gandhi?
content.note: The Poona Pact (1932) was an agreement between Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi. It abandoned the idea of separate electorates for 'Depressed Classes' in favor of reserved seats in provincial legislatures.

content.question: Who founded the Forward Bloc in 1939?
content.note: Subhas Chandra Bose founded the Forward Bloc in 1939 as a faction within the Indian National Congress after resigning from the presidency due to ideological differences with Gandhi.

content.question: Where did the Quit India Movement begin?
content.note: The Quit India Movement was launched on August 8, 1942, from the August Kranti Maidan (then Gowalia Tank Maidan) in Mumbai.

content.question: Who founded the All India Depressed Classes Association?
content.note: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar founded the All India Depressed Classes Association in 1930 to represent the interests of Dalits and demand political rights within the British Indian administration.

content.question: Which Mughal ruler was involved in the Revolt of 1857?
content.note: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), the last Mughal Emperor, was proclaimed the leader of the Revolt of 1857 by the sepoys. After the revolt's failure, he was exiled to Rangoon by the British.

content.question: Who was the first Indian elected to the British Parliament?
content.note: Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian to be elected as a Member of Parliament (MP) in the British House of Commons (1892–1895), representing the Liberal Party.

content.question: Who wrote India Wins Freedom?
content.note: India Wins Freedom is an autobiographical narrative by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, India's first Education Minister, providing an insider's view of the partition and independence.

content.question: What was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact related to?
content.note: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) resulted in the suspension of the Civil Disobedience Movement and allowed Congress to participate in the Second Round Table Conference in London.

content.question: In which year did Alfonso de Albuquerque capture Goa?
content.note: In 1510 CE, the Portuguese admiral Alfonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur, making it the headquarters of the Portuguese State of India for centuries.

content.question: In which year did the Surat Split occur?
content.note: The Surat Split occurred in 1907 during the INC session, where the party divided into two factions: the Moderates (led by Gokhale) and the Extremists (led by Tilak).

content.question: Which was the first nationwide Satyagraha launched by Gandhi?
content.note: The Rowlatt Act Satyagraha (1919) was Gandhi's first nationwide protest. It was launched against the 'Black Act,' which allowed the government to imprison political activists without trial.

content.question: Who was known as the Grand Old Man of India?
content.note: Dadabhai Naoroji is revered as the 'Grand Old Man of India.' He is famous for his 'Drain of Wealth' theory, which explained how Britain was systematically looting India's economy.

content.question: Who founded the Indian Association in 1876?
content.answer: Surendranath Banerjee and Anand Mohan Bose
content.note: Surendranath Banerjee and Anand Mohan Bose founded the Indian Association in 1876. It was one of the most important pre-Congress nationalist organizations in British India.

content.question: Who was the first female president of the Indian National Congress?
content.note: The Irish socialist and theosophist Annie Besant became the first woman president of the Indian National Congress at the Calcutta session in 1917.

content.question: Who founded the Servants of India Society?
content.note: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, the political guru of Mahatma Gandhi, founded the Servants of India Society in 1905 to train Indians to devote their lives to the cause of the country.

content.question: Who founded the newspaper Kesari?
content.note: Bal Gangadhar Tilak founded the Marathi newspaper Kesari. He used its columns to criticize British policies and spread nationalist ideas among the masses.

content.question: Who was a founder of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association?
content.note: Chandra Shekhar Azad was a key leader and reorganizer of the HSRA (Hindustan Socialist Republican Association) in 1928, aiming for an independent socialist republic through armed revolution.

content.question: Where did Gandhi organize a Satyagraha for mill workers in 1918?
content.note: In 1918, Gandhi led the Ahmedabad Mill Strike. It was significant as his first use of a hunger strike as a political weapon to help workers secure a 35% wage hike.

content.question: In which language was Gulamgiri written?
content.note: Gulamgiri (Slavery), a powerful book critiquing the caste system and dedicated to the American movement to abolish slavery, was written by Jyotirao Phule in Marathi.

content.question: In which year was the World Parliament of Religions held in Chicago?
content.note: The World Parliament of Religions took place in 1893 in Chicago, where Swami Vivekananda gave his historic speech beginning with 'Sisters and brothers of America'.

content.question: In which year was the Indian Councils Act (Morley-Minto Reforms) passed?
content.note: The Indian Councils Act of 1909, known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, is infamous for introducing separate electorates for Muslims, sowing the seeds of communalism.

content.question: During whose tenure was the Indian Universities Act, 1904 passed?
content.note: The Indian Universities Act (1904) was passed during the tenure of Lord Curzon to bring universities under tighter government control following the recommendations of the Raleigh Commission.

content.question: When was the first English factory established in Bengal?
content.note: The English East India Company established its first factory in Bengal at Hooghly in 1651 CE, under the permission of Sultan Shuja, the Governor of Bengal.

content.question: In which year was the Diwani of Bengal granted to the East India Company?
content.note: Following the Battle of Buxar, the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani Rights (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha to the EIC in 1765 CE.

content.question: Who was the last Governor-General of the East India Company?
content.note: Lord Canning was the last Governor-General appointed by the East India Company and became the first Viceroy of India after the Government of India Act 1858.

content.question: Who returned his knighthood after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
content.note: Rabindranath Tagore renounced his Knighthood in 1919 as a symbolic protest against the brutal Jallianwala Bagh Massacre in Amritsar.

content.question: Who introduced the Ryotwari system?
content.note: Thomas Munro (along with Alexander Reed) introduced the Ryotwari System in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies. Under this, revenue was collected directly from the Ryots (cultivators).

content.question: When did Vasco da Gama discover the sea route to India?
content.note: The Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on the Malabar Coast in 1498 CE, opening the direct sea route from Europe to India via the Cape of Good Hope.

content.question: In which year was the Treaty of Salbai signed?
content.note: The Treaty of Salbai was signed in 1782, ending the First Anglo-Maratha War. it resulted in a period of relative peace between the Marathas and the British for twenty years.

content.question: Which princely state was first annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse?
content.note: Satara was the first princely state to be annexed by the British in 1848 through the application of Lord Dalhousie's controversial Doctrine of Lapse.

content.question: Against which country was the Opium War fought using Indian sepoys?
content.note: The Opium Wars (1839–1860) were fought between Britain and China. The British used Indian sepoys and resources from the British Indian Army to force China to allow the opium trade, which was largely cultivated in India.

content.question: Where was the national anthem first sung in 1911?
content.note: The national anthem, Jana Gana Mana, was first sung on December 27, 1911, during the Kolkata (Calcutta) session of the Indian National Congress. It was composed by Rabindranath Tagore.

content.question: Who was the INC president in 1915?
content.note: Satyendra Prasad Sinha (Lord Sinha) presided over the 1915 Bombay Session of the INC. He was notably the first Indian to become a member of the Viceroy's Executive Council and the first Indian peer in the British House of Lords.

content.question: Who introduced the Blue Water Policy?
content.note: Francisco de Almeida, the first Portuguese Viceroy in India, introduced the Blue Water Policy. The goal was to establish Portuguese naval supremacy in the Indian Ocean rather than building a land-based empire.

content.question: What were cotton fabrics from Calicut called in Europe?
content.note: The cotton fabrics exported from Calicut (modern-day Kozhikode) to Europe were known as Calico. This term eventually became a general name for all Indian cotton textiles in Western markets.

content.question: What was the oldest Dutch settlement in India?
content.note: The Dutch East India Company established its oldest and most significant settlement at Pulicat (Tamil Nadu) in 1610. They built Fort Geldria here, which served as their headquarters on the Coromandel Coast.

content.question: What fort did the British build in Calcutta?
content.note: The British East India Company built Fort William in Calcutta (Kolkata) to protect their factory and trading interests. It was named after King William III of England and later became the seat of the Bengal Presidency.

content.question: Which places were major British trading centers in India?
content.note: The British established their major trading centers (Presidency towns) at Surat (first factory), Madras (Fort St. George), Bombay (received as dowry), and Calcutta (Fort William).

content.question: Who founded the independent Bengal state?
content.note: Murshid Quli Khan, originally appointed as the Diwan of Bengal by Aurangzeb, became the first independent Nawab of Bengal. He shifted the capital from Dacca to Murshidabad.

content.question: Which treaty ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War?
content.note: The Treaty of Mangalore (1784) ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War. It was signed between Tipu Sultan and the British East India Company, with both parties agreeing to restore captured territories and prisoners.

content.question: Which region was given to the British under the Treaty of Srirangapatnam?
content.note: Under the Treaty of Srirangapatnam (1792), which ended the Third Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu Sultan had to cede half of his kingdom, including the Malabar region, to the British and their allies.

content.question: Which region was known as Kala Pani?
content.note: The Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands was known as Kala Pani ('Black Water'). It was used by the British to exile political prisoners and revolutionaries to a remote, inescapable location.

content.question: Where is Srirangapatnam Fort located?
content.note: Srirangapatnam Fort is located on an island in the Cauvery River in the state of Karnataka. It was the historic capital of Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan.

content.question: Who started the Revolt of 1857?
content.note: The Revolt of 1857 was ignited by the sepoys (Indian soldiers) of the British East India Company's army at Meerut. The immediate cause was the introduction of the Enfield rifle, which was rumored to use greased cartridges offending both Hindus and Muslims.
